content: The document contains references to various studies, guidelines, and expert opinions on iodine fortification, salt iodization, and related public health interventions. 1. Guidelines for the prevention of cardiovascular disease emphasize the importance of assessing and managing cardiovascular risk factors. These guidelines were accessed on June 19, 2014. 2. The global strategy on diet, physical activity, and health was discussed during the Fifty-seventh World Health Assembly in Geneva from May 17 to 22, 2004. The resolutions and decisions from this assembly were accessed on June 18, 2014. 3. Ohlhorst et al. (2012) reviewed the use of iodized salt in processed foods across various countries and highlighted the role of food processors in ensuring adequate iodine levels. This study was published in the Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety. 4. De Jong (2014) conducted a review on the use of iodized salt in processed foods, with the findings accessed on June 20, 2014. 5. West and Merx examined the effects of iodized salt on the color and taste of food, with their findings accessed on June 19, 2014. 6. Kojima and Brown (1955) investigated the effects of iodized salt on processed fruits and vegetables, publishing their findings in Food Technology. 7. Kuhajek and Fiedelman (1973) explored the nutritional iodine content in processed foods, with their research appearing in Food Technology. 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidelines on fortifying food-grade salt with iodine to prevent and control iodine deficiency disorders. These guidelines were accessed on June 19, 2014. 9. Wang et al. (1999) studied the effects of storage and cooking on iodine content in iodized salt and proposed methods for monitoring iodine levels. Their research was published in Biomedical and Environmental Sciences. 10. Diosady et al. (1998) evaluated the stability of iodine in iodized salt used to address iodine deficiency disorders. Their findings were published in the Food and Nutrition Bulletin. 11. Goindi et al. (1995) estimated iodine losses during various cooking procedures, with their research published in the Asia Pacific Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 12. Maramag et al. (2007) assessed the stability of iodine in fresh and aged iodized salt under simulated market conditions. Their findings were published in the Food and Nutrition Bulletin. 13. Shawel et al. (2010) highlighted post-production losses in iodine concentration in salt, which hinder efforts to control iodine deficiency disorders. This case study focused on Northern Ethiopia and was published in the Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition. 14. Winger et al. (2005) addressed technological challenges associated with iodine fortification of foods in a report prepared for the New Zealand Food Safety Authority. 15. Higgins and Green edited the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, providing a framework for evaluating evidence quality and intervention effectiveness. 16. Aburto et al. (2014) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the effects and safety of salt iodization to prevent iodine deficiency disorders. This review was published by the WHO eLibrary of Evidence for Nutrition Actions. 17. Haas et al. (2014) demonstrated the efficacy of double-fortified salt in improving iron deficiency indicators among female Indian tea pickers. Their study was published in the Journal of Nutrition. 18. The Salt Institute provided information on iodized salt, with their resources accessed on September 10, 2014. 19. WHO and UNICEF outlined acceptable medical reasons for using breast-milk substitutes in a 2009 publication. 20. WHO and UNICEF issued a joint statement on achieving optimal iodine nutrition in pregnant and lactating women and young children, accessed on June 19, 2014. 21. Angermayr and Clar (2009) reviewed iodine supplementation for preventing iodine deficiency disorders in children, with their findings published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 22. Ghassabian et al. (2014) investigated the relationship between maternal urinary iodine concentration during pregnancy and children's cognitive outcomes in an iodine-sufficient population. Their findings were published in BMJ Open. 23. The WHO Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition Information System (VMNIS) provides data on micronutrient deficiencies, including iodine, to support public health interventions. 24. The WHO guideline on fortifying food-grade salt with iodine emphasizes its effectiveness in preventing iodine deficiency disorders, with recommendations based on evidence quality ranging from very low to moderate. 25. The WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development oversees the creation of evidence-based recommendations to address global nutrition challenges. 26. WHO experts and advisory panels provide guidance on public health policies, including salt iodization and iodine supplementation, to address micronutrient deficiencies. 27. The GRADE Working Group evaluates the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations, emphasizing the importance of high-quality research to inform public health interventions. 28. WHO guidelines highlight the cost-effectiveness and feasibility of salt iodization as a public health intervention, noting its long-standing success in reducing iodine deficiency disorders globally. 29. The WHO emphasizes the need for strong monitoring and reporting mechanisms to ensure the benefits of salt iodization outweigh potential harms at the population level. 30. WHO and other international organizations collaborate to address micronutrient deficiencies in emergency-affected populations, emphasizing the importance of iodine fortification in such contexts. 31. The WHO Nutrition for Health and Development (NHD) department, led by Dr. Francesco Branca, focuses on addressing global nutrition challenges, including iodine deficiency disorders. 32. WHO experts in various fields, including maternal and child health, HIV/AIDS, and environmental health, contribute to the development and implementation of public health guidelines. 33. The WHO guideline development process involves a thorough review of evidence, expert consultations, and consideration of feasibility, cost, and potential harms to ensure effective public health interventions.
